question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer is explaining to a first-time LP why 'Lotus India Growth AIF' (Cat II) uses a pooled vehicle instead of managing each investor's money in a separate portfolio. Which of the following is the MOST accurate rationale for pooling in an AIF context?

answer.text: Pooling guarantees each investor a separately managed, customised mandate (like PMS) with individual portfolio statements.
Pooling is a SEBI-mandated requirement only for Category III AIFs and is optional for Category I and II.
Pooling eliminates the need for the manager to draft a Private Placement Memorandum (PPM) because all investors share a single mandate.
Pooling combines investor contributions into a common corpus to achieve economies of scale, risk diversification and collective investment management ('blind-pool investing').

explanation.text: The Logic: Pooling is central to AIF structuring. Investor contributions are combined into a common corpus (a 'blind pool') managed under a single mandate, enabling economies of scale, broader strategy and risk diversification. Individual customisation is the hallmark of PMS, not pooled AIFs. SEBI AIF Regulations 2012 require pooling across all three categories. The Trap: The PMS-like option confuses pooling with portfolio management (XXI-B territory). The Cat III-only option wrongly carves out Cat I/II. PPM waiver is false - PPM is mandatory regardless of pooling. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (Portfolio Managers) tests the OPPOSITE - individual portfolios, no pooling. XIX-A/B test pooling from distributor angle. XIX-D tests it from the Manager's desk where pooling drives fund economics. Manager's Pro-Tip: When pitching to an LP who has only seen PMS before, emphasise the 'blind-pool + pass-through' combo: pooled investing gives diversification and scale, while Cat I/II enjoy pass-through under Section 115UB so the LP isn't worse off tax-wise.
